title: VINYL DROP: Twelve records, one Friday, no repress, a record store release kit (preorder email, drop page, printed invoice and stock-sheet PDF, cover-art cards from one drop file)
body:
### Which challenge are you entering?
Hyper Elements Template Challenge (November 2026)

### Project name
VINYL DROP: Twelve records, one Friday, no repress, a record store release kit (preorder email, drop page, printed invoice and stock-sheet PDF, cover-art cards from one drop file)

### Project description

One drop file in → **12 personalised preorder emails, a 5-page printed invoice and stock-sheet PDF, a public drop page and 13 cover-art cards** out, from one theme and one set of shared components.

A release drop's paperwork fails in a predictable way: the email says one thing, the wall sheet another, and the sleeve in the customer's hand says a third, a different pressing, a different price, a catalogue number spelled two ways. This kit makes that impossible by construction. Every catalogue number, pressing and price lives in one drop file: the email quotes it, the page's cards carry it, and the printed invoice prints it next to the owner's note.

- **Preorder email** (`Email` → `render()`), the news leads: your copy is reserved for pickup or shipping, with the pressing scarcity, the order total and the catalogue stamp. No Svg, no remote images: the DropStrip (one square per release, hot red and the release's stock colour) is a `Row` of fixed-width `Column`s, so it survives image-blocking inboxes. The table is the compact five-column form, because a 600px email cannot hold seven columns without squeezing the record names; the pressing and stock are already in the prose. `MergeTag` greeting; plain-text twin from the same render.
- **Drop page** (`Page` → `render()`), black hero, the twelve-release drop strip, every release as a typed `vinyl.ReleaseCard` grouped by stock status (7 in stock, 3 low stock, 2 sold out), the low-stock watch list, phone styles, no client-side JavaScript.
- **Printed invoice and stock sheet** (`Document` → `renderPdf()`), the record pinned behind the counter: page one is the drop itself (numbers, how to read a release), pages two to four are the twelve releases, four to a page, page five is the invoice totals, the low-stock watch list and the owner's note. `PageHeader`/`PageFooter` with `PageNumber`. No browser makes this PDF.
- **Cover-art cards** (`Canvas` → `renderImage()`), 1080×1080 PNGs: the drop cover, plus one card per release with artist, title, blurb and pressing numbers in poster type. Server-rendered; fonts in as bytes; nothing fetched.

**Measured on the demo run (22 Nov 2026):** 12 preorder emails · 5 invoice pages in one PDF · 13 cover cards · 12 releases, 3,800 copies pressed, 882 on the shelf, 1,069 preorders · $28,403 in preorders, $14,641 of stock on the shelf · **gate: 0 errors, 0 warnings** · full batch in **2.4s**.

**Corrections pass:** drop data is deterministic (no clock, no randomness), so fixing one record re-renders only that record, the other 11 emails are byte-identical.

### Public GitHub repository URL
https://github.com/dunoil/vinyl-drop

### How did you use Hyper Elements?

- **One `defineTheme()`** carries all four roots, black, cream paper, hot red for shapes only, dark red for text accents, mono catalogue numbers, Inter bold headings with tight letter spacing, per-format overrides: the Document and the Canvas are forced to Inter because satori only draws the font bytes it is given. One deliberate constraint shaped it: phone styles are an error in a Document or a Canvas, so the theme carries no `mobile` blocks, Email/Page templates set their own.
- **Shared components across roots** (`Wordmark`, `DropStrip`, `DropLine`, `ReleaseTable`, `LowStockList`) are why the emailed pressing and the printed one are the same pressing.
- **The mark is built from layout primitives on purpose.** An Email cannot hold an Svg, so the DropStrip is Rows of fixed-width Columns, and it recolours automatically per release, because the squares are data on the releases. A 12-cell strip overflows a hero column, so it splits into rows of 12; the gate's layout check caught that before it shipped.
- **A custom element with `defineElement()`**: `vinyl.ReleaseCard` with typed props (`prop.text`). A mistyped catalogue number or a missing price is a diagnostic with a path, before anything renders.
- **`validate()` as a gate, not a linter.** The batch validates before writing a single file. `out/checks.json` makes the verdict a file instead of a claim.
- **`@hyper-elements/email-clients`** for client proof (`npm run clients`): 5 previews of the email as classic Outlook, Gmail and Apple Mail draw it; screenshots in `docs/`.
- **CLI-ready**: `npx hyper-elements check templates/` reports **4 templates: 0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 skipped** (verified 22 Nov 2026).
- **Written for agents too** (`AGENTS.md`): ten invariants an agent must not break.

**Run it:** `npm install && npm run check && npm run render && npm run make` (12 emails) · `npm run make:sample` (4) · `npm run clients`. Node 20+. `examples/` holds one artefact of each kind.

### Live preview URL (optional)
No hosted preview. `examples/` in the repository contains the preorder email (HTML + plain text), the drop page, the printed invoice and stock sheet as a PDF and the cover card PNG, all from the demo run, and `docs/` holds screenshots of every output, including the email as Outlook and Gmail render it.

### Which challenge are you entering?

Hyper Elements Template Challenge (November 2026)

### Project name

Kerbside

### Project description

**The timetable your stop used to have on paper.** Drop in any transit operator's GTFS feed and pick a stop. Kerbside reads which services run on each day of the week you choose and makes:

- a stop poster (PDF, A4): each line at the stop with its departures by hour for Monday to Friday, Saturday and Sunday, footnotes worked out ("a: Fridays only")
- an email of the times, for someone who won't use the app: every bus by hour, first and last bus per day
- a lock-screen image (PNG, 1080 × 1920) of one line's weekday times, readable with no signal

### Public GitHub repository URL

https://github.com/rohit-jsfreaky/kerbside

### How did you use Hyper Elements?

The three outputs are **Hyper Elements templates** in `templates/`. The app renders them in the browser (`src/lib/render-route.ts`, so the site runs on Cloudflare as static files), and the CLI renders the same files.

- **Typed fields with rules:** every minute must look like `05` or `35a` (a footnote letter), hours are 0–23, route colours are `#RRGGBB`, one to four lines, up to 24 hours each. Values outside the rules stop the render with the field and the reason.
- **`<Document>` + `renderPdf()`** for the A4 stop poster in Overpass (a typeface after the US highway signs) and Overpass Mono: the stop's name on a signage-blue band with its lines' route boxes, then a striped table per line, coloured with the route's colour from the feed. Pages are planned from the row counts, because a Document page doesn't flow by itself.
- **`<Email>`** with `Table`, `TableRow` and `TableCell` for the times, lint (`lang`, `contrast`, `link-text`), the email client checks and preview text required (the weekday first and last buses).
- **`<Canvas>` + `renderImage()`** for the 1080 × 1920 lock screen, with `image/overflow`, `image/glyph` and `image/fit` required: the top third stays empty for the phone's clock, and the row size is worked out from the number of hours so the day always fits.
- **Values files + CLI:** `npm run sheets` turns `docs/sample.json` into values files with `hyper-elements design new`, then renders all three with `hyper-elements render`.

### Which challenge are you entering?

Hyper Elements Template Challenge (November 2026)

### Project name

Cousins

### Project description

**The family tree on one page. Aunts and uncles included.** Load your GEDCOM export from Ancestry, FamilySearch or MyHeritage. Cousins puts a couple, their children and their grandchildren on one printable page, hides living people's dates, and writes the email that asks the family to fill the gaps:

- a family chart (PDF), A3 or A4 landscape, one page, sized to fit
- the same chart as an image (PNG) for the family chat
- a "help fill the gaps" email listing who's missing a birthplace, a date of death…, never living people

### Public GitHub repository URL

https://github.com/rohit-jsfreaky/cousins

### How did you use Hyper Elements?

The three outputs are **Hyper Elements templates** in `templates/`. The app renders them in the browser (`src/lib/render-route.ts`, so the site runs on Cloudflare as static files), and the CLI renders the same files.

- **The tree is laid out with Hyper Elements primitives.** `templates/_shared/doc.tsx` works out each family's width from its children, puts boxes in `Row`s and `Column`s, and draws the lines from parents to children with `Svg` + `Line`. Wide families switch to an outline: the youngest generation is listed downward under each parent, on a `Column` border with `Svg` ticks. The chart picks whichever layout gives the bigger scale for the space (the A3 page uses the outline, the wide image spreads across).
- **Formats.** The chart template has two `formats`, `a3` and `a4` landscape, and reads the format in `render` to size the tree to the page.
- **Typed fields with rules:** 2–4 generations, at most 80 people in the chart and 30 gaps, names capped so boxes stay readable.

### Project name

Homeward

### Project description

**When a pet goes missing, fill in one file. You get the whole appeal: a big poster with tear-off phone tabs, a card for local groups, an email for shelters and vets, and an updates page. When your pet comes home, change one word and every piece turns into a thank-you.**

https://github.com/rohit-jsfreaky/homeward

### How did you use Hyper Elements?

Hyper Elements does the whole job here, not just the drawing. The four outputs are **templates** (`@hyper-elements/react/template`), and the CLI is the engine that runs them.

- **One root per output.** `<Document>` for the poster (rendered to PDF), `<Canvas>` for the card (PNG), `<Email>` for the appeal email, `<Page>` for the updates page.
- **Formats.** The poster template has three `formats` (`tabloid`, `letter`, `a4`) with their own layout sizes, so one values file gives three PDFs.

- **Values files and the CLI.** `scripts/appeal.mjs` runs `hyper-elements design new` once per template, which turns `pet.json` into checked values files in `appeal/`, then runs `hyper-elements render appeal/`. ### Which challenge are you entering?

Hyper Elements Template Challenge (November 2026)

### Project name

MobiPay

### Project description

MobiPay renders one mobile money receipt as an email, web page, PDF and PNG from a single transaction, built with Hyper Elements. It handles successful, pending, failed and reversed payments, with wording that explains what happened and what the sender should do next.

The receipts include recipient and network details, fees, UTC timestamps and transaction references. Debits and refunds follow the recorded amounts, with principal and fee refunds shown separately. The demo includes GHS, NGN and USD samples, two configurable brands, phone layouts and downloadable files.

![MobiPay demo](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/iamIniunam/mobipay/main/docs/preview.gif)

### Public GitHub repository URL

https://github.com/iamIniunam/mobipay

### How did you use Hyper Elements?

The receipt is written once in `src/receipt/body.ts`, as a function of the transaction, brand and font family, using `Column`, `Row`, `Heading`, `Text` and `Link`. Each output wraps that same body in a different root:

| Output | Root | Renderer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Email | `Email` | `render()` |
| Web page | `Page` | `render()` |
| PDF | `Document` | `renderPdf()` |
| PNG | `Canvas` | `layoutImage()`, then `renderImage()` |

`render()` also runs in the browser, which is how the demo draws the email and web receipts live. The download files are generated in Node for 24 sample combinations: 2 brands × 3 currencies × 4 statuses. Email includes a plain-text version.

A few notes from building with it:

- PDF and PNG use explicit Inter TTF files. Email and web use a font stack, with Inter loaded into the demo's preview frame.
- The PNG export measures the body with `layoutImage()` before drawing it. Strict rendering checks for overflow, so longer names and notes can increase the image height.
- Phone styles apply to the HTML outputs. PDF and PNG use the same body with fixed padding and type sizes.

To run it, use Node 22, clone the repo, then run `npm ci` and `npm run dev`. `npm run render` regenerates the samples. The README includes setup, customisation and renderer details.

Built with React, TypeScript, Vite, `@hyper-elements/react` 0.5.2 and Inter. AI assistance: I used Claude while building the first version, and Codex for review, refinements, testing and submission preparation.

### Which challenge are you entering?
Hyper Elements Template Challenge (November 2026)

### Project name
MEND — Bring the broken thing: a repair café kit (customer email, workshop page, printed repair-ticket PDF, status-and-parts cards from one session file)

### Project description

One session file in → **40 personalised customer emails, a 7-page printed repair-ticket PDF, a public workshop page and 5 status-and-parts cards** out — from one theme and one set of shared components.

A repair session's paperwork fails in a predictable way: the email says one thing, the wall sheet another, and the ticket in the customer's hand says a third — a different diagnosis, a different fixer, a ticket number spelled two ways. This kit makes that impossible by construction. Every ticket number, diagnosis and fixer lives in one session file: the email quotes it, the page's cards carry it, and the printed tickets print it next to the host's note.

- **Customer email** (`Email` → `render()`) — the verdict leads: fixed and ready for pickup, awaiting a part, or honestly beyond repair. The diagnosis the fixer wrote at the bench, the fixer, the parts, the pickup instructions and the donation thank-you follow. No Svg, no remote images: the BenchStrip (one square per ticket, safety orange and the ticket's status colour) is a `Row` of fixed-width `Column`s, so it survives image-blocking inboxes. `MergeTag` greeting; plain-text twin from the same render.
- **Workshop page** (`Page` → `render()`) — wood-dark hero, the forty-ticket bench strip, every ticket as a typed `repair.TicketCard` grouped by status (27 fixed, 9 awaiting parts, 4 beyond repair), the fixer roster and the parts on order, phone styles, no client-side JavaScript.
- **Printed repair tickets** (`Document` → `renderPdf()`) — the record pinned to the workshop wall: page one is the session itself (numbers, fixers, how to read a ticket), pages two to six are the forty tickets, eight to a page, page seven is the parts on order, the donations and the host's note. `PageHeader`/`PageFooter` with `PageNumber`. No browser makes this PDF.
- **Status-and-parts cards** (`Canvas` → `renderImage()`) — 1080×1080 PNGs: the session cover, one card per status and the parts card, led by that status in poster type. Server-rendered; fonts in as bytes; nothing fetched.

**Measured on the demo run (21 Nov 2026):** 40 customer emails · 7 ticket pages in one PDF · 5 status cards · 27 fixed, 9 awaiting parts, 4 beyond repair · $200 in donations · **gate: 0 errors, 0 warnings** · full batch in **1.6s**.

**Corrections pass:** ticket data is deterministic (no clock, no randomness), so fixing one record re-renders only that record — the other 39 emails are byte-identical.

### Public GitHub repository URL
https://github.com/dunoil/mend

### How did you use Hyper Elements?

- **One `defineTheme()`** carries all four roots — warm wood, steel grey, safety orange for shapes only, cream paper, mono ticket numbers, Inter bold headings, per-format overrides: the Document and the Canvas are forced to Inter because satori only draws the font bytes it is given. One deliberate constraint shaped it: phone styles are an error in a Document or a Canvas, so the theme carries no `mobile` blocks — Email/Page templates set their own.
- **Shared components across roots** (`Wordmark`, `BenchStrip`, `SessionLine`, `TicketTable`, `FixerList`, `PartsList`) are why the emailed diagnosis and the printed one are the same diagnosis.
- **The mark is built from layout primitives on purpose.** An Email cannot hold an Svg, so the BenchStrip is Rows of fixed-width Columns — and it recolours automatically per ticket, because the squares are data on the tickets. A 40-cell strip overflows a hero column, so it splits into rows of 20; the gate's layout check caught that before it shipped.
- **A custom element with `defineElement()`**: `repair.TicketCard` with typed props (`prop.text`). A mistyped ticket number or a missing diagnosis is a diagnostic with a path, before anything renders.
- **`validate()` as a gate, not a linter.** The batch validates before writing a single file. `out/checks.json` makes the verdict a file instead of a claim.
- **`@hyper-elements/email-clients`** for client proof (`npm run clients`): 5 previews of the email as classic Outlook, Gmail and Apple Mail draw it; screenshots in `docs/`.
- **CLI-ready**: `npx hyper-elements check templates/` reports **4 templates: 0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 skipped** (verified 21 Nov 2026).
- **Written for agents too** (`AGENTS.md`): ten invariants an agent must not break.

**Run it:** `npm install && npm run check && npm run render && npm run make` (40 emails) · `npm run make:sample` (6) · `npm run clients`. Node 20+. `examples/` holds one artefact of each kind.

The brand is Foldline, a fictional paper shop where every gift card is a piece of folded paper. A shop can drop in its own name, links and terms. Values that would break an output are refused with a sentence a shop can show beside the field: a name too wide for the card, an emoji no printer can draw, a note too long for a share image. https://github.com/YashM2704/foldline-gift-cards

  - `Email` (HTML and plain text), and `Page` for the balance page.

- **Text measured from the fonts' own glyph widths.** The same TrueType files the renderers use are measured once into a table, so templates fit amounts, names and notes exactly, and set every line break on images and PDFs themselves.
- **Fonts:** single TTF files per weight from fonts.gstatic.com in each root's `fonts` prop.

### Project name

NEXORA Signature — Universal Business Report Studio

### Project description

NEXORA Signature is an executive business intelligence and universal business reporting studio built with React, TypeScript, and Hyper Elements.

It transforms a single validated business data model into five synchronized output formats: Email HTML, Plain-Text Email, Responsive Web HTML, A4 PDF, and High-Resolution PNG.

The platform includes executive insights, rolling three-month trend analysis, interactive business simulations, audience-specific report editions, financial data redaction, customizable branding, email compatibility auditing, and an export quality scorecard.

Its goal is to make professional business reporting consistent, customizable, and accessible across multiple delivery formats.

### Public GitHub repository URL

https://github.com/Thanusha8095/nexora-signature

### How did you use Hyper Elements?

NEXORA Signature is built using the official `@hyper-elements/react` package (v0.5.0). I integrated Hyper Elements as the core rendering and document-generation layer, defining eight reusable custom elements with `defineElement()` and configuring a shared visual system with `defineTheme()`.

The implementation uses Hyper Elements' Email, Page, Document, and Canvas roots to support multiple report formats from a consistent report model. I also use its validation and design utilities, including `validate()`, `outline()`, and `toDesign()`, alongside `renderPdf()` and `renderImage()` for document exports.

This integration allows NEXORA to generate consistent, audience-specific business reports across responsive web, HTML email, plain-text email, PDF, and PNG formats.

body: ### Which challenge are you entering? Hyper Elements Template Challenge (November 2026) ### Project name The Listing — The Real Estate Kit ### Project description ### What I built Property listings hide their maths — a headline price, a super built-up area nobody lives in, charges that surface at registration. **The Listing** ("Drawn to measure") is a complete real-estate kit designed as an architect's drawing sheet: ivory drafting paper, charcoal ink, one oxblood accent, hairline rules and dimension lines — and one centerpiece, a floor plan drawn entirely in code from the room data. It covers one fictional property end to end — Skyline Residency, Tower B, Unit 1102, Whitefield, Bengaluru, an east-facing 3 BHK asking ₹1.85 crore: - **Email (600)** — new-listing alert + open-house invite: masthead, price panel, facts grid, "the plan, in words" (the same room data as ruled area rows, since email gets no Svg), the computed money, oxblood open-house band - **Page (1120)** — the listing page in four numbered sections: the code-drawn plan with dimension strings, title block and north arrow; the room schedule with share bars; the cost sheet with loan panel and locality gauge; the visit section - **Document (A4, 2 pages)** — brochure & cost sheet: plan, key figures and the verdict on page 1; the room schedule and the full arithmetic on page 2, with real page numbers - **Canvas (1080×1350)** — the poster (PNG + SVG): the drawing sheet itself — plan as hero, price block with the "Sheet A-101" stamp, measured cost strip, oxblood open-house band ### One listing file, everything computed All four templates render from a single listing file in `src/data.ts`, and none of the figures is typed in by hand. Thirteen rooms are defined by position and size in feet; their areas are width × depth, computed — the carpet rooms sum to **1,450 sq ft**, and the 230 sq ft balcony is drawn and scheduled but excluded per RERA, giving a **carpet efficiency of 78.4%** against the 1,850 sq ft plate. Price per sq ft is shown both ways — **₹12,759 on carpet, ₹10,000 on super built-up**. Against a Whitefield average of ₹11,900, the listing computes to **+7.2%**, which crosses the +5% band in code and produces the verdict the sheet prints: **"At a premium"** — stated, not hidden. Karnataka stamp duty (5.65%) and registration (1%) are applied to the price for a **total acquisition of ₹1,97,30,250**, and the loan is genuinely amortised — 80% at 8.5% over 20 years → **EMI ₹1,28,438/month**, total interest ₹1,60,25,081. Change the price, a room's width, the duty rate or the loan share and the plan redraws and every figure re-derives in all four formats. ### How Hyper Elements is used - All four roots — `Email`, `Page`, `Document`, `Canvas` — from one `defineTheme()` and a shared component library (keystone wordmark, mastheads, ruled cost rows, sheet stamp, locality gauge, floor-plan renderer). The plan is a composition of `Layer`, layout and `Svg`: room cells' borders are the walls, and a per-room Svg overlay carries door-swing arcs built from line segments, window bands and drawn fixtures. The Email gets an Svg-free variant of the art. - `validate()` gates the build; the Document renders via `renderPdf()` and the Canvas via `renderImage()`, with real Cormorant Garamond/Inter/JetBrains Mono font files passed as bytes. - The email was checked with `@hyper-elements/email-clients`: **7 client previews** (Outlook, Outlook.com, Gmail, Apple Mail, iPhone) are generated by the build into `out/email-clients/`. **Validation: 0 errors, 0 warnings on all four templates** (the email carries 39 informational notes — classic Outlook letter-spacing, font-weight and button-hover notes — nothing broken). ### Run it ```bash npm install npm run build # validates, then renders everything into out/ npm run check # validate only ``` All names, the property, the firm, the prices and the rates are fictional sample data — Skyline Residency doesn't exist, but the next time a listing quotes me a super built-up area, I'll ask for the drawing sheet. 📐 ### Public GitHub repository URL https://github.com/Aayu095/The-Listing-The-Real-Estate-Kit ### How did you use Hyper Elements? All four roots — Email, Page, Document, Canvas — are built from one defineTheme() and a shared component library (keystone wordmark, mastheads, ruled cost rows, sheet stamp, locality gauge, floor-plan renderer). The plan is a composition of Layer, layout and Svg: room cells' borders are the walls, and a per-room Svg overlay carries door-swing arcs built from line segments, window bands and drawn fixtures. The Email gets an Svg-free variant of the art. validate() gates the build; the Document renders via renderPdf() and the Canvas via renderImage(), with real Cormorant Garamond/Inter/JetBrains Mono font files passed as bytes. The email was checked with @hyper-elements/email-clients: 7 client previews (Outlook, Outlook.com, Gmail, Apple Mail, iPhone) are generated by the build into out/email-clients/. title: CURTAIN CALL — One night, every seat filled: a community theatre production kit (patron email, production page, printed programme PDF, cast cards from one production file)
body:
### Which challenge are you entering?
Hyper Elements Template Challenge (November 2026)

### Project name
CURTAIN CALL — One night, every seat filled: a community theatre production kit (patron email, production page, printed programme PDF, cast cards from one production file)

### Project description

One production file in → **60 personalised patron emails, a 2-page printed programme, a public production page and 8 cast cards** out — from one theme and one set of shared components.

A production's paperwork fails in a predictable way: the email says one thing, the website another, and the programme in the audience's hands says a third — a different date, a different price, a cast member spelled two ways. This kit makes that impossible by construction. Every date, price and name lives in one production file: the email quotes it, the page's cards carry it, and the printed programme prints it next to the director's note.

- **Patron email** (`Email` → `render()`) — the three nights lead, in their own performance table, before the ticket tiers. No Svg, no remote images: the CurtainStrip (one fold per cast member, burgundy and gold alternating) is a `Grid` of `Column`s, so it survives image-blocking inboxes. `MergeTag` greeting; plain-text twin from the same render.
- **Production page** (`Page` → `render()`) — burgundy hero with a serif display title, every cast member as a typed `stage.CastMember` card with a billing stamp, phone styles, no client-side JavaScript.
- **Printed programme** (`Document` → `renderPdf()`) — the record handed to every seat: page one is the night itself (synopsis, three performances, ticket tiers), page two is the company (cast table, crew, the director's note). `PageHeader`/`PageFooter` with `PageNumber`; Times serif headings. No browser makes this PDF.
- **Cast cards** (`Canvas` → `renderImage()`) — 1080×1080 PNGs, one per cast member, led by that character in poster type with an "On stage with…" line, plus the company card. Server-rendered; fonts in as bytes; nothing fetched.

**Measured on the demo run (19 Nov 2026):** 60 patron emails · 2 programme pages in one PDF · 8 cast cards · **gate: 0 errors, 0 warnings** · full batch in **2.1s**.

**Corrections pass:** patron generation is deterministic (no clock, no randomness), so fixing one record re-renders only that record — the other 59 emails are byte-identical.

### Public GitHub repository URL
https://github.com/dunoil/curtain-call

### How did you use Hyper Elements?

- **One `defineTheme()`** carries all four roots — warm cream paper, ink black, deep burgundy velvet and gold, a serif display face against Inter body, named `card`/`stamp`/`mono`/`goldRule` styles, Button variants, per-format overrides: the Document gets Times headings, the Canvas is forced to Inter because satori only draws the font bytes it is given. One deliberate constraint shaped it: phone styles are an error in a Document or a Canvas, so the theme carries no `mobile` blocks — Email/Page templates set their own.
- **Shared components across roots** (`Wordmark`, `CurtainStrip`, `PerformanceLine`, `PerformanceTable`, `TicketTable`, `CastTable`) are why the emailed performance date and the printed one are the same date.
- **The mark is built from layout primitives on purpose.** An Email cannot hold an Svg, so the CurtainStrip is a Grid of Columns — and it recolours automatically per production, because the folds are data on the cast.
- **A custom element with `defineElement()`**: `stage.CastMember` with typed props (`prop.text`, `prop.choice`). A mistyped billing is a diagnostic with a path, before anything renders.
- **`validate()` as a gate, not a linter.** The batch validates before writing a single file. `out/checks.json` makes the verdict a file instead of a claim.
- **`@hyper-elements/email-clients`** for client proof (`npm run clients`): 5 previews of the email as classic Outlook, Gmail and Apple Mail draw it; screenshots in `docs/`.
- **CLI-ready**: `npx hyper-elements check templates/` reports **4 templates: 0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 skipped** (verified 19 Nov 2026).
- **Written for agents too** (`AGENTS.md`): ten invariants an agent must not break.

**Run it:** `npm install && npm run check && npm run render && npm run make` (60 emails) · `npm run make:sample` (6) · `npm run clients`. Node 20+. `examples/` holds one artefact of each kind.

### Live preview URL (optional)
No hosted preview. `examples/` in the repository contains the patron email (HTML + plain text), the production page, the printed programme as a PDF and the cast card PNG, all from the demo run — and `docs/` holds screenshots of every output, including the email as Outlook and Gmail render it.

body:
### Which challenge are you entering?

Hyper Elements Template Challenge (November 2026)

### Project name

Hyper Invoice

### Project description

An invoice template where one JSON file produces everything a freelancer or studio sends to a client:

- **Email** (HTML + plain text) to send the invoice, with the amount and due date as the inbox preview
- **Web page** the client can open from a link, which adapts to phones
- **PDF** (A4) for printing and records, with fonts embedded and identical bytes for the same invoice
- **Social card** (1200×630 PNG/SVG) so a shared payment link previews with the amount due

![Invoice email](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Ashish-CodeJourney/hyper-invoice/main/docs/email.png)

| PDF (A4) | Web page on a phone | Social card |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ![PDF](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Ashish-CodeJourney/hyper-invoice/main/docs/pdf.png) | ![Phone](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Ashish-CodeJourney/hyper-invoice/main/docs/mobile.png) | ![Card](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Ashish-CodeJourney/hyper-invoice/main/docs/card.png) |

What makes it practical:

- **Money done right.** Amounts are integers in the currency's minor unit, so totals never drift. Currency and dates follow the invoice locale (`$1,234.56`, `1.234,56 €`, `￥5,000`, `3 December 2026`).
- **Safe input.** `parseInvoice()` checks untrusted JSON with a Zod schema and returns readable errors such as `lineItems.0.quantity: Too small: expected number to be >0`.
- **One command.** `npm run build -- my-invoice.json` writes all five files.
- **Tested.** 48 tests, 100% coverage, mutation-tested with Stryker. Approval tests keep the rendered email, page, print layout and card under review, so any visual change shows up in a diff.

### Public GitHub repository URL

https://github.com/Ashish-CodeJourney/hyper-invoice

### How did you use Hyper Elements?

- **One layout, four roots.** `InvoiceContent` is a plain component. `<Email>`, `<Page>`, `<Document>` and `<Canvas>` each wrap it or a card built from the same data.
- **All three renderers.** `render()` for the email and page, `renderPdf()` with Inter embedded for the PDF, and `renderImage()` for the PNG/SVG card.
- **One theme for every output.** `defineTheme()` holds the colours, fonts, element defaults and named styles (`card`, `label`, `dueSummary`), with `token()` references.
- **Per-output changes from the theme.** `formats.document` switches the PDF to a white, tighter layout that saves ink. `mobile` styles stack the header and parties on phones in the email and page.
- **Layout elements.** `Row`, `Column` and `Table` with `header`/`footer` rows, `cellPadding` and `rowBorder`, plus `Button` and `Divider`.
- **Metadata from the invoice.** `previewText`, `description`, `title` and `lang` come from the invoice data, so inbox previews and link previews show who it's from, the amount and the due date.

The landing page puts the typeface itself at the centre, with animated typography, interactive weight demonstrations, scrolling text and a horizontal specimen gallery. I wanted it to feel like an actual type foundry website rather than another generic marketing template.

Hyper Elements is the core of Meridian. I used it to build one reusable component system that can generate five different outputs without having to design each one separately.

### Project description

One water file in → **120 personalised member notices, a 6-page rotation-chart PDF, a public season page and 6 gate cards** out — from one theme and one set of shared components.

A subak is the cooperative that has shared Bali's spring water across the rice terraces for a thousand years, by rules (awig-awig) agreed at the water temple. Water is the one thing a village cannot argue about twice: if the notice in a farmer's inbox gives their block 22% of the spring and the chart pinned at the bale says 20%, the argument happens at the gate. This kit makes disagreement impossible by construction — and its central rule is the subak's own: **a block's water share is its share of the land**. `shareOf()` computes every share from the areas in the file (the six shares sum to exactly 100.0%), so no output anywhere can quote a share a person typed.

- **Member notice email** (`Email` → `render()`) — each farmer's own block first (its computed share, window, lead), the flowing blocks called out, then the full rotation everyone agreed at the temple. No Svg, no remote images: the PolengMark — saput poleng, the checked cloth of balance — is a `Row` of `Column`s, so the notice survives image-blocking inboxes. `MergeTag` greeting ("Om Swastiastu"); plain-text twin from the same render.
- **Season page** (`Page` → `render()`) — a deep-forest hero with real `Svg` terrace art (allowed here, forbidden in the email), every block as a typed `subak.BlockCard`, and the fairness rule stated where everyone can read it. No client-side JavaScript.
- **Rotation charts** (`Document` → `renderPdf()`) — one A4 chart per block, printed for the bale where the subak meets: the block's share and window, its **member list with gate-watch duties**, and the pekaseh's signature line. No browser makes this PDF.
- **Gate cards** (`Canvas` → `renderImage()`) — 1080×1080 PNGs, one per block, its share and window as the heroes on a deep forest ground. Server-rendered; fonts in as bytes; nothing fetched.

**Measured on the demo run (19 Nov 2026):** 120 member notices · 6 rotation charts in one 6-page PDF · 6 gate cards · **gate: 0 errors, 0 warnings** · full batch in **3.0s**.

**Corrections pass:** farmer generation is deterministic (no clock, no randomness), so fixing one record re-renders only that record — the other 119 notices are byte-identical.

https://github.com/dunoil/subak

### How did you use Hyper Elements?

- **One `defineTheme()`** carries all four roots — frangipani cream, deep forest ink, terrace green, gold leaf, Georgia display over an Inter body, named `card`/`stamp`/`mono` styles, Button variants, per-format overrides. The theme carries no `mobile` blocks on purpose — phone styles are an error in a Document or a Canvas.

### Project description

One harvest file in → **120 personalised box emails, one 120-page packing PDF, a public box page and 8 recipe cards** out — from one theme and one set of shared components.

The point is not "four outputs". It is that each destination gets a job only it can do, and the box a subscriber reads about is provably the same box the packer packs, because it is the same component tree under four roots:

- **Box email** (`Email` → `render()`) — the weekly letter. Drawn entirely with tables underneath. No Svg, no remote images: the HarvestMark (one cell per crop, in harvest order) is a `Grid` of `Column`s, so a subscriber whose client blocks images still sees their whole harvest. `MergeTag` personalises the greeting; the plain-text twin comes from the same render.
- **Box page** (`Page` → `render()`) — the public page. The lush one: full `Svg` field art, a `Grid` of typed `ProduceCard`s, phone styles, no client-side JavaScript.
- **Packing slips** (`Document` → `renderPdf()`) — a real print job: A4, `PageHeader`/`PageFooter` with `PageNumber`, one `Document.Page` per box, a 30px collation code (`S34-001`) readable across a barn, and packer notes written for a human with a pen. No browser makes this PDF.
- **Recipe cards** (`Canvas` → `renderImage()`) — 1080×1350 PNGs, one per crop, each flooding its field-art band with that crop's colour. Server-rendered; fonts in as bytes; nothing fetched.

**Measured on the demo run (18 Nov 2026, from `out/batch.json` and `out/checks.json` in the repo's own run):** 120 boxes · 120 personalised emails (HTML + plain text) · 120 packing pages in one PDF · 8 recipe cards · **gate: 0 errors, 0 warnings** · full batch in **6.4s**.

**Corrections pass:** subscriber generation is deterministic (no clock, no randomness), so fixing 3 boxes re-renders only those 3 — the other 117 emails and slips are byte-identical.

### Public GitHub repository URL
https://github.com/dunoil/sown-harvest-kit

- **One `defineTheme()`** carries all four roots — colour roles, a Georgia/Inter pairing, a three-step heading scale, `card`/`stamp` named styles, Button variants, and per-format overrides (square buttons for email, smaller quiet type for print). One engine doing the work the library was built for, not four templates with a shared palette: - **One `defineTheme()`** carries all four roots — colour roles, a three-step heading scale, `badge` and `stamp` named styles, per-element defaults. Change one token and every email, page, PDF and PNG follows. - **Shared components across roots** (`Weave`, `WeaveSpec`, `Wordmark`, `Stamp`) are why the printed badge and the emailed badge are the same badge. - **The art is built from layout primitives on purpose.** An `Email` cannot hold an `Svg`, so the weave is a `Grid` of `Column`s with a background colour — and it flips to a knocked-out variant (`tone="ink"`) for the story card's ink band. - **`Document` as a real imposition**: `orientation="landscape"`, `margin` insets, a `Grid` of three, `PageFooter` with `` and ``, plus per-slot collation markers. - **`renderPdf()` and `renderImage()` on the server** — no browser, no screenshot service, no network. 240 cards are 240 renders, not 240 tabs; font bytes go in through the `fonts` option. - **`validate()` as a gate, not a linter someone remembers to run.** Before the first email is written, a sample of each output runs `validate()` with the `lint()` plugin *and* `emailClients()`. An error stops the run, so 240 versions of one mistake never reach disk; `checks.json` makes the gate's verdict a file instead of a claim. - **`@hyper-elements/email-clients`** for the client proof (`npm run clients`): the same email previewed as classic Outlook, Gmail and Apple Mail draw it. Result: 5 previews, **2 degradations** — a button's `borderRadius` goes square in Outlook and `hover` doesn't fire. Nothing else moved. - **`@hyper-elements/cli` in the loop**: `templates/` holds one default-exported component per output, so `npx hyper-elements check templates/` reports **4 templates: 0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 skipped**. - **Written for agents too** (`AGENTS.md`): the invariants an agent must not break and the exact failure that produced each one. What the engine's diagnostics actually caught while building this: `
` in `Text` (→ `LineBreak`), `marginTop` (no margins exist), `alignItems: "flex-start"`, `justifyContent` in an email (classic Outlook starts children at the left), a **2.88:1 accent** on paper (→ a darkened text ink at 4.9:1, bright ink kept for shapes), and one-weight fonts asked for another weight. Two things it could not catch, both fixed: `№` rendered as a tofu box in the story card (no such glyph in Space Mono), and the first unconstrained weave was *unique* but produced solid and twinned rows — **21 of 240 names** — which is now a hard `assertWeave()` invariant the batch throws on, keeping every badge in a 50–77% ink band. **Run it:** `npm install && npm run make` (240 attendees, ~2m20s) · `npm run check` · `npm run corrections` · `npm run shots`. Node 22+. `examples/` holds one artifact of each kind for reviewers who would rather not run anything. ### Live preview URL (optional) No hosted preview. `examples/` in the repository contains the welcome email (HTML + plain text), the badge page, the story card PNG, sheet 1 as a PDF and the corrections outputs, all from the demo run. ### Submission confirmation - [X] I have starred the [Hyper Elements repository](https://github.com/hyper-elements/hyper-elements). - [X] My repository is public and contains the complete source code and required README. - [X] My submission meets the requirements of the selected challenge.

body:
**Repo:** https://github.com/Ankith-m1006/rent-receipt-kit

![Rent Receipt Kit: the receipt email, the A5 PDF receipt with its counterfoil, the WhatsApp image and the year's HRA statement](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Ankith-m1006/rent-receipt-kit/master/docs/kit.png)

Every year, millions of salaried people in India have to give their employer rent receipts to claim House Rent Allowance. Most of those receipts still come from a stationery-shop receipt book, filled in by hand one month at a time. HR sends them back if the landlord's PAN is missing.

**Rent Receipt Kit** turns one `tenancy.ts` file into:

- **a receipt email** for each month (`Email` → `render()`)
- **a printable A5 receipt PDF** with the counterfoil the landlord keeps (`Document` → `renderPdf()`)
- **a WhatsApp image** of the receipt, 1080×1350, because that's where landlords and tenants actually talk (`Canvas` → `renderImage()`, drawn at 540×675 with `scale: 2`)
- **the year's HRA statement** for payroll: an A4 PDF with every month, the total, the landlord's PAN, a declaration and page numbers (`Table`, `PageFooter`, `PageNumber`)
- **the tenant's web page**, showing the year at a glance, with every receipt one tap away (`Page`, `Grid`)

**How Hyper Elements is used**

- **One `ReceiptSlip` component is drawn into all four destinations,** so the email, page, PDF and image can never disagree about an amount, a date or a PAN.
- **One `defineTheme` theme carries the receipt-book look:** pink carbon paper, a printed maroon header band, a red serial number, ballpoint entries in Kalam, `₹18,500/-` in a box, and a purple rubber PAID stamp. The perforated edge is an `Svg` of circles in the PDF and image, and a dotted border in the email and page.
- **`validate()` runs in the build** and fails on errors. It caught two of my mistakes: `space-between` in email, and phone styles inside a `Document`. That's why the slip knows which destination it's drawn into.

**India's rules, built in (with tests)**

- The landlord's PAN appears once the year's rent is above ₹1,00,000.
- A ₹1 revenue stamp box appears only on cash receipts above ₹5,000.
- Amounts are written in lakh and crore ("One Lakh Forty Eight Thousand"), with Indian grouping (₹2,22,000).
- The financial year runs April to March, with receipt numbers per year (`R-2026-27/03`).
- There's no receipt for a month that isn't paid.

**Run it**

```bash
npm install
npm run build   # validates, then writes every email, PDF, image and the page to out/
npm test        # the rent rules
```

All names, the PAN and the payment references in the sample are invented.

Dark header band with a `v1.0 · LIVE` badge, hero with a release card as the visual, a three-card feature grid, "What's new in 1.0", a testimonial strip, a dark early-access band, and a footer with social links and unsubscribe.

### How did you use Hyper Elements?

The whole point of this entry is Hyper Elements' core value — **"React in. Everything out."** The announcement is written once as a shared content component and renders as three outputs from one React template:

- **Email** — the default export under an `Email` root (the template the gallery shows)
- **Web page** — the same content under a `Page` root (responsive, no client JavaScript)
- **Printed document** — the same content paginated across two A4 pages under a `Document` root, rendered to PDF with `renderPdf()`

One `defineTheme` theme carries the brand (slate ink, one indigo accent, Inter) into every root. Components used throughout: `Email` / `Page` / `Document`, `Column` / `Row` / `Grid` layout, `Heading`, `Text`, `Button`, `Link`, `List`, `Menu` and `Social` — no raw HTML, no `html` prop.
